readings.orig: καὶ εἰσελεύσεται Σεδεκίας εἰς Βαβυλῶνα καὶ ἐκεῖ καθιεῖται
readings.en: Zedekiah will go into Babylon, and there he will sit
readings.plain: Zedekiah will go into Babylon, and there he will stay.

why: No Qumran scroll preserves the verse, and the Greek's shorter text could be an abridgment or a different edition. The Plain follows the Hebrew, as the longer and fuller text, and notes that the Greek lacks the clause that makes Zedekiah's stay end with a divine visit.
b: The Greek does not say how long Zedekiah stays, and it has no warning to the Judeans about fighting. If the Greek is an earlier edition, the longer text added the "visit" and the warning. If the Greek abridged, it cut them. The Plain cannot decide between these.

readings.orig: οὐ μὴ ἀποκρυβῇ ἀπὸ σοῦ οὐθέν
readings.en: nothing will be hidden from you
readings.plain: Nothing at all will be hidden from you.

why: The Hebrew word matches Genesis 18:14, the verse Jeremiah is quoting. The Greek may be a loose rendering of the same verb, or may reflect a different understanding of the root. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek uses the same "hidden" at 32:27 (Greek 39:27). Both Greek verses make the claim about God's knowledge, not about his power to do wonders. Genesis 18:14 in Greek says "Will anything be impossible with God?", so the Greek translator of Jeremiah did not use that verse.

why: The Hebrew is the phrase of Deuteronomy 26:8 (mora' gadol, 'great terror'; Deuteronomy 4:34 has the plural, moraim gedolim). The Greek of Deuteronomy 26:8 and 4:34 renders the same phrase with the same words found here, 'great visions' (en horamasin megalois), so the Greek of Jeremiah follows the Greek Deuteronomy. This is a difference of translation, not of the Hebrew text, and the Plain follows the Hebrew.

why: No Qumran scroll preserves this verse. The Greek lacks the whole passage (33:14–26). The Plain follows the Hebrew and records the Greek's absence.
b: The Old Greek has Jeremiah 33:1-13 and then goes straight to the Hebrew chapter 34 (Greek 41). Swete's Codex Vaticanus and, as Tov reports, Ziegler's critical text lack all thirteen verses. Scholars who hold that the Greek translates an earlier, shorter edition read the passage as a later addition; those who hold that the Greek abridged read it as original. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c is a witness to the longer text for verses 16 to 20 only.

a: then I might also reject the offspring of Jacob and of David my servant, and not take from his offspring rulers over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But I will turn their fortunes around, and I will have compassion on them."
p: The Old Greek lacks this verse, like all of 33:14-26. See 33:14.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: גַּם־זֶ֣רַע יַעֲקוֹב֩ וְדָוִ֨ד עַבְדִּ֜י אֶמְאַ֗ס מִקַּ֤חַת מִזַּרְעוֹ֙ מֹֽשְׁלִ֔ים אֶל־זֶ֥רַע אַבְרָהָ֖ם יִשְׂחָ֣ק וְיַעֲקֹ֑ב כִּֽי־אָשִׁ֥יב אֶת־שְׁבוּתָ֖ם וְרִחַמְתִּֽים׃ ס
readings.en: then I might also reject the offspring of Jacob and of David my servant, and not take from his offspring rulers over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But I will turn their fortunes around, and I will have compassion on them."
readings.plain: then I might also reject the offspring of Jacob and of David my servant, and not take from his offspring rulers over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But I will turn their fortunes around, and I will have compassion on them."

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek none; Greek 40 ends at the Hebrew 33:13)
readings.en: (not in the Greek)

why: No Qumran scroll preserves this verse. The Greek lacks the whole passage (33:14–26). The Plain follows the Hebrew and records the Greek's absence.

a: As burnings were made for your fathers, the earlier kings who came before you, so people will make a burning for you, and they will mourn for you, "Alas, lord!"
t: Burnings and 'Alas, lord!', or weeping 'to Hades'
p: The Greek has weeping where the Hebrew has burnings, no 'Alas, lord!', and adds 'to Hades'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: בְּשָׁל֣וֹם תָּמ֗וּת וּֽכְמִשְׂרְפ֣וֹת אֲ֠בוֹתֶיךָ הַמְּלָכִ֨ים הָרִֽאשֹׁנִ֜ים אֲשֶׁר־הָי֣וּ לְפָנֶ֗יךָ כֵּ֚ן יִשְׂרְפוּ־לָ֔ךְ וְה֥וֹי אָד֖וֹן יִסְפְּדוּ־לָ֑ךְ כִּֽי־דָבָ֥ר אֲנִֽי־דִבַּ֖רְתִּי נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃
readings.en: In peace you will die, and like the burnings of your fathers, the earlier kings who were before you, so they will burn for you, and 'Alas, lord!' they will lament for you, for I have spoken a word, the LORD declares.
readings.plain: As burnings were made for your fathers, the earlier kings who came before you, so people will make a burning for you, and they will mourn for you, "Alas, lord!"

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 41:5)
readings.orig: Ἐν εἰρήνῃ ἀποθανῇ· καὶ ὡς ἔκλαυσαν τοὺς πατέρας σου τοὺς βασιλεύσαντας πρότερόν σου, κλαύσονται καὶ σέ, καὶ ἕως ᾅδου κόψονταί σε· ὅτι λόγον ἐγὼ ἐλάλησα, εἶπεν Κύριος.
readings.en: You will die in peace. As they wept for your fathers who reigned before you, they will weep for you, and they will beat their breasts for you as far as Hades, for I have spoken a word, says the LORD.
readings.plain: As people wept for your fathers who reigned before you, they will weep for you, and they will mourn you as far as Hades.

why: No Qumran scroll preserves this verse. The Greek has no burnings and no 'Alas, lord!' and adds 'as far as Hades'; whether it abridged or translated a different Hebrew cannot be told. The Plain follows the Hebrew, and the note on this verse discusses the burnings.

a: At the end of seven years
p: The Greek has 'when six years are completed'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: from the end of seven years
readings.plain: At the end of seven years

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 41:14)
readings.en: When six years are completed
readings.plain: When six years are completed

why: The Hebrew can be read as the law of Deuteronomy 15:12 (six years of service, release in the seventh). The Greek states the six years directly. The Plain follows the Hebrew and puts the Greek in the note.
b: The Hebrew agrees with the seventh-year release (a national date, as Sarna argued) or with the individual law, depending on how it is read. The Greek is closer to Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 as individual laws.

a: a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth
p: The Greek has 'scattering', and 'death' for 'plague'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Ketiv and Qere differ only in spelling (zeva'ah, za'avah)
readings.en: a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth
readings.plain: a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 41:17)
readings.orig: εἰς διασπορὰν πάσαις ταῖς βασιλείαις τῆς γῆς
readings.en: to scattering among all the kingdoms of the earth
readings.plain: a scattering among all the kingdoms of the earth

why: 'Terror to all the kingdoms' is a regular curse phrase in Jeremiah (15:4; 24:9; 29:18). The Greek 'scattering' is an interpretation. The Greek also reads 'death' (thanatos) where the Hebrew has 'disease' (deber).

a: into the calf they cut in two and passed between its pieces
p: In Swete's Greek the calf is not cut in two, and no one passes between the pieces.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: הָעֵגֶל אֲשֶׁר כָּרְתוּ לִשְׁנַיִם וַיַּעַבְרוּ בֵּין בְּתָרָיו
readings.en: the calf that they cut in two and passed between its pieces
readings.plain: into the calf they cut in two and passed between its pieces

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 41:18)
readings.orig: τὸν μόσχον ὃν ἐποίησαν ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτῷ
readings.en: the calf which they made to serve it
readings.plain: the calf they made to serve

why: The Hebrew describes the rite of Genesis 15. The Greek has a different and much shorter text with no cutting. It may be a misreading or a different edition. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
b: The next verse shows the same minus in the Greek: it has no clause about those who passed between the pieces (see 34:19).

a: who passed between the pieces of the calf
t: Those who passed between the pieces
p: The Greek lacks the clause that the officials passed between the calf's pieces.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: who passed between the pieces of the calf
readings.plain: who passed between the pieces of the calf

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 41:19)
readings.orig: τοὺς ἄρχοντας Ἰούδα καὶ τοὺς δυνάστας καὶ τοὺς ἱερεῖς καὶ τὸν λαόν
readings.en: the rulers of Judah, the powerful men, the priests and the people
readings.plain: the leaders of Judah, the powerful men, the priests and the people

why: The Hebrew completes the list of those who swore with the clause about passing between the pieces. The Greek has a shorter list, with no calf and no passing. See 34:18. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah
t: The names of the Rechabite leader and his family
p: The Greek has 'Jechoniah' for Jaazaniah and other forms of the fathers' names.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah
readings.plain: Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 42:3)
readings.en: Jechoniah son of Jeremin, son of Chabasein
readings.plain: Jechoniah son of Jeremin, son of Chabasein

why: In the next verse the Greek also has 'Jonan son of Ananias son of Godolias' where the Hebrew has Hanan son of Igdaliah, and 'Selom' for Shallum. These are different forms of names, and which is original cannot be told. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: and the army of Aram
p: The Greek has 'the army of the Assyrians'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and from before the army of Aram
readings.plain: and the army of Aram

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 42:11)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπὸ προσώπου τῆς δυνάμεως τῶν Ἀσσυρίων
readings.en: and from before the army of the Assyrians
readings.plain: and the army of the Assyrians

why: 2 Kings 24:2 names Aramean raiders among the force sent against Jehoiakim, which fits the Hebrew. The Greek 'Assyrians' may be the translator's guess or may rest on a Hebrew text that read differently; the evidence does not decide. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: fifth year
p: The Greek has the eighth year of Jehoiakim for the fast.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: in the fifth year
readings.plain: fifth year

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 43:9)
readings.en: in the eighth year
readings.plain: eighth year

why: The fifth year (604 BC) is a year after the scroll was written (36:1) and fits a fast in the ninth month, when the Babylonian army took Ashkelon. The Greek date is the only other witness, and the Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: were not afraid
p: The Greek has 'did not inquire' where the Hebrew has 'were not afraid'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and they were not afraid
readings.plain: were not afraid

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 43:24)
readings.en: and they did not inquire
readings.plain: did not inquire

why: The Greek verb means 'seek, inquire'; it may be a loose rendering or may translate a different Hebrew verb. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which matches the king's contempt in the rest of the verse.

a: also pleaded with the king not to burn the scroll
t: Pleaded not to burn, or urged to burn
p: The Greek reverses the sense: two officials suggest to the king that he burn the scroll.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: also pleaded with the king not to burn the scroll
readings.plain: also pleaded with the king not to burn the scroll

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 43:25)
readings.orig: ὑπέθεντο τῷ βασιλεῖ πρὸς τὸ κατακαῦσαι τὸ χαρτίον
readings.en: suggested to the king to burn the scroll
readings.plain: suggested to the king that he burn the scroll

why: The Greek names two officials, not three, says they urged the burning, and has no 'he did not listen to them'. The Hebrew fits the officials' fear in 36:16 and their warning to Baruch in 36:19. The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Greek here is Swete's Codex Vaticanus; no Qumran scroll preserves the verse.

a: But the LORD hid them.
t: The LORD hid them, or 'they were hidden'
p: The Greek has the passive 'they were hidden' and no mention of the LORD.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the LORD hid them
readings.plain: But the LORD hid them.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 43:26)
readings.en: and they were hidden
readings.plain: But they were hidden.

why: The Hebrew names the LORD as the one who protects Jeremiah and Baruch. The Greek is shorter, as it often is with divine names in Jeremiah.

a: in place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim
p: The Greek says Zedekiah ruled in place of Jehoiakim, with no Coniah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: in place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim
readings.plain: in place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 44:1)
readings.en: in place of Jehoiakim
readings.plain: in place of Jehoiakim

why: Zedekiah took the throne after Jehoiachin (Coniah), Jehoiakim's son (2 Kings 24:17). The Greek skips a generation.

a: to claim a share there among the people
p: The Greek has 'to buy from there'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: to share a share from there in the midst of the people
readings.plain: to claim a share there among the people

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 44:12)
readings.orig: τοῦ ἀγοράσαι ἐκεῖθεν ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ λαοῦ
readings.en: to buy from there among the people
readings.plain: to buy something there among the people

why: The Hebrew verb halaq, 'divide', is common; the difficulty is its sense with 'from there' (mishsham). The Greek 'to buy' reads it as a statement about trading. The Plain follows the Hebrew and gives the other readings in the note on 37:12.

a: a captain of the guard named Irijah son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah
p: The Greek has no 'captain of the guard' and names the man Sarouia, not Irijah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: בַּעַל פְּקִדֻת וּשְׁמוֹ יִרְאִיָּיה בֶּן־שֶׁלֶמְיָה בֶּן־חֲנַנְיָה
readings.en: a master of oversight, and his name Irijah son of Shelemiah son of Hananiah
readings.plain: a captain of the guard named Irijah son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 44:13)
readings.orig: ἄνθρωπος παρ᾽ ᾧ κατέλυεν Σαρουιὰ υἱὸς Σελεμίου υἱοῦ Ἁνανίου
readings.en: a man with whom he lodged, Sarouia son of Selemias son of Ananias
readings.plain: a man with whom he lodged, Sarouia son of Selemias, son of Ananias

why: The father's and grandfather's names agree (Selemias is Shelemiah, Ananias is Hananiah); the man's own name and his title differ. Which is original cannot be told, and no Qumran scroll preserves the verse. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashhur son of Malkijah
p: The Greek lists three names and changes the first.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: שְׁפַטְיָה בֶן־מַתָּן וּגְדַלְיָהוּ בֶן־פַּשְׁחוּר וְיוּכַל בֶּן־שֶׁלֶמְיָהוּ וּפַשְׁחוּר בֶּן־מַלְכִּיָּה
readings.en: Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashhur son of Malkijah
readings.plain: Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashhur son of Malkijah

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 45:1)
readings.orig: Σαφανίας υἱὸς Ναθὰν καὶ Γοδολίας υἱὸς Πασχὼρ καὶ Ἰωαχὰλ υἱὸς Σελεμίου
readings.en: Saphanias son of Nathan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur and Joachal son of Selemias
readings.plain: Zephaniah son of Nathan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur and Jucal son of Shelemiah

why: The Hebrew is the fuller list. The Greek lacks Pashhur son of Malkijah and has a different first name.

a: by the sword, by famine and by disease
p: The Greek lacks 'plague'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: by the sword, by famine and by disease
readings.plain: by the sword, by famine and by disease

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 45:2)
readings.en: by the sword and by famine
readings.plain: by the sword and by famine

why: Sword, famine and plague is Jeremiah's usual triad (21:9; 24:10; 27:8; 32:24). The Greek often has only two.

a: a court official
p: The Greek has no 'court official'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: a court official
readings.plain: a court official

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 45:7)
readings.en: Abdemelech the Ethiopian
readings.plain: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian

why: Ebed-melech's rank as a sarîs is in the Hebrew only. The Greek leaves out the title, which may be an abridgment.

a: these men have done evil in everything they have done to Jeremiah the prophet. They threw him into the cistern, and he will die where he is, of hunger, for there is no more bread in the city
p: In Swete's Greek Ebed-melech speaks to the king directly: 'you have done evil'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: הֵרֵעוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה אֵת כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂוּ לְיִרְמְיָהוּ הַנָּבִיא
readings.en: these men have done evil in all they have done to Jeremiah the prophet
readings.plain: these men have done evil in everything they have done to Jeremiah the prophet. They threw him into the cistern, and he will die where he is, of hunger, for there is no more bread in the city

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 45:9)
readings.orig: Ἐπονηρεύσω ἃ ἐποίησας τοῦ ἀποκτεῖναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ λιμοῦ, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν ἔτι ἄρτοι ἐν τῇ πόλει
readings.en: You have done evil in what you did, to kill this man because of the famine, for there are no more loaves in the city
readings.plain: you have done evil in what you did, putting this man to death because of the famine, for there is no more bread in the city

why: In the Hebrew the king is not accused; the officials are. In the Greek he is (the verb is second person). The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: The men at peace with you have misled you and overpowered you. Your feet have sunk in the mud, and they have turned back.
p: The Greek taunt looks ahead ('will prevail', 'will settle your feet in slippery places') where the Hebrew looks back.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: הִסִּיתוּךָ וְיָכְלוּ לְךָ אַנְשֵׁי שְׁלֹמֶךָ הָטְבְּעוּ בַבֹּץ רַגְלֶךָ נָסֹגוּ אָחוֹר
readings.en: They misled you and overpowered you, the men of your peace; your feet were sunk in the mud, they turned back
readings.plain: The men at peace with you have misled you and overpowered you. Your feet have sunk in the mud, and they have turned back.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 45:22)
readings.orig: Ἠπάτησάν σε, καὶ δυνήσονταί σοι ἄνδρες εἰρηνικοί σου, καὶ καταλύσουσιν ἐν ὀλισθήμασιν πόδας σου, ἀπέστρεψαν ἀπὸ σοῦ.
readings.en: They deceived you, and the men at peace with you will prevail over you, and they will bring your feet to rest in slippery places; they turned away from you.
readings.plain: They deceived you, and the men at peace with you will prevail over you, and will set your feet down in slippery places. They turned away from you.

why: The Greek renders 'mud' (bots) as 'slippery places' and uses future verbs for the first two. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: And it happened, when Jerusalem was captured...
p: The Greek ends the chapter at 'until the day Jerusalem was captured'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and it was, when Jerusalem was captured
readings.plain: And it happened, when Jerusalem was captured...

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint), as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (Greek 45:28)
readings.en: (the chapter ends)

why: The Hebrew clause leads into 39:3 in the Hebrew text; the Greek does not have that passage (39:4–13).
